opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The core reason is that mathematics is one of the very few domains where we can have a perfect verifier. If you write a proof in a formal system like Lean or HOL Light, a computer can check it with essentially complete certainty. That means you have an environment where an AI system can practice, make attempts, and get an unambiguous signal about whether it succeeded. It's a bit like Go or chess, except the space is open-ended and essentially unlimited in depth.

The problem is that almost all of human mathematical knowledge isn't written in formal language. It's in papers, textbooks, and lecture notes, in natural language with a lot of implicit context, notational conventions, and "it's easy to see" steps. Formal libraries, as impressive as they are, cover only a tiny fraction of what mathematicians know. Manually formalizing everything would take an enormous number of person-years, so if we want a system to reason at the frontier, we can't wait for humans to do it.

Autoformalization is the bridge. If a system can read informal mathematics and translate it into formal statements and proofs, two things happen. First, you unlock that whole corpus of human knowledge as training data and as a library the system can build on. Second, you create a self-improving loop: the system translates, tries to prove things, the verifier tells it what's correct, and that feedback improves both the translation and the reasoning. Even imperfect translations are useful, because the formal checker filters out the garbage, and you're left with a growing body of verified results.

There's also a deeper point. I believe that once you have a system that can reliably move between informal intuition and formal rigor, you have something that resembles how a strong mathematician actually works: you think intuitively and loosely, and then you nail it down. Combining the creativity of large language models with the hard grounding of formal verification is, in my view, the most plausible path to a system that doesn't just imitate mathematics but genuinely exceeds human ability. And mathematics is a good proving ground for that, because verified reasoning there could carry over to things like software verification and other areas where correctness really matters.

r001.rationale: It proposes translating informal mathematics to unlock the existing corpus as a library and grow verified results, expanding the supply of verifiable mathematical material.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the fundamental reason is that mathematics is the one domain where we can actually verify whether a reasoning step is correct, with essentially no ambiguity, as long as it's written in a formal language. If you have a proof in something like Lean or Isabelle or HOL Light, a small, trusted kernel can check it, and either it goes through or it doesn't. That gives you a perfect reward signal, which is extremely rare. In most of the areas where we train these systems, the feedback is noisy, or it comes from humans, who are slow, expensive, and often wrong. In formal mathematics, the environment itself tells you the truth.

The problem is that almost all of the mathematics humanity has produced lives in natural language, in papers and textbooks, with a lot of implicit context and hand-waving that a human reader fills in. The formal corpora that exist today are tiny by comparison, maybe a few hundred thousand theorems across all the proof assistants, written by a small community over decades. So if you want to train a system that reasons at or beyond the level of a strong mathematician, you simply don't have enough formal data to do it directly.

Autoformalization is the bridge. The idea is to have a system that reads informal mathematics and translates it into a precise, machine-checkable form. Once you can do that reliably, several things happen at once. First, you unlock the entire existing body of mathematical knowledge as training signal, because every statement you formalize becomes something you can try to prove, and every proof you find can be verified. Second, you get a closed loop. The system can propose conjectures, formalize them, attempt proofs, check them, and learn from the outcome without a human in the loop. That's the kind of self-improvement cycle that I think is necessary for getting to superhuman performance. Humans are the bottleneck everywhere else.

And third, it changes how we interact with the results. If a model hands you a hundred-page informal argument, you have to trust it, or spend months checking it. If it hands you a formal proof, you don't have to trust anything except a kernel that's a few hundred lines long. So autoformalization is not just a route to stronger systems, it's a route to systems whose outputs we can actually rely on, which I think becomes very important as they get more capable than we are.

I'd also say that the skills involved are more general than they look. Translating fuzzy human intent into something precise, with the right assumptions made explicit, is essentially what good engineers and scientists do all the time. So I've always thought of mathematics as the cleanest testbed for a capability that eventually generalizes to things like verified software and formal reasoning about the real world.

astra-6.text:
I see autoformalization as a bridge between the way we communicate mathematics and the way a computer can verify it. Mathematicians work in natural language, with a lot of intuition and implicit assumptions. A formal system requires you to make those assumptions precise, and then it can check whether your proof actually follows from them.

That gives you a very powerful learning signal. If a model produces a convincing-looking argument in natural language, it can be difficult to tell whether it is correct. But if it produces a formal proof, you can check it mechanically. The model can propose ideas, try different approaches, and learn from failures, while the proof checker provides a reliable constraint.

Autoformalization is important because so much mathematical knowledge is expressed informally. If we can translate that knowledge into a form that machines can work with, we can connect learning from existing mathematics with searching for new proofs. And eventually, you can imagine a feedback loop where the system proposes conjectures, proves some of them, and uses those results to tackle harder problems.

Of course, verification alone doesn’t tell you which problems are interesting or which concepts will be useful. You still need creativity and good judgment. But I think combining that kind of learned intuition with rigorous verification is a promising route to systems that can go beyond human mathematical capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics gives us a particularly useful setting because we can check whether an argument is correct. If you want a system to go beyond what humans can do, you eventually reach a point where a human cannot reliably judge its answers. With formal mathematics, a proof checker can verify a proof even if finding that proof required much more intelligence than we have.

But most of our mathematical knowledge is written in informal language. Autoformalization is the bridge: it translates mathematical statements and arguments into a language where the computer can check them. That would let us connect the enormous amount of existing mathematical knowledge with automated reasoning.

The exciting possibility is a feedback loop. A system proposes a conjecture or a proof, formalizes it, checks it, and learns from the failures. It can generate new, verified examples rather than depending entirely on examples written by humans. Autoformalization alone does not solve mathematical intelligence, but it could make that kind of scalable, self-improving process possible.
